slides.title: Executive summary

paragraphs.text: Executive summary
Keep buying housings in 2027, add a qualified second source and hold the leased cell as a gated option for 2028; the owned cell cannot be funded within the board's limits
Like for like, the owned cell's $27 saving per housing shrinks to about $1.70
–	Operating savings repay only 78% of the $7.3M outlay by 2029
–	Over 2027–29 the owned cell saves $0.51M and the lease $0.30M
The owned cell breaks the board's limits, and the lease needs near-full demand
–	The $7.3M outlay tops the $5.0M limit and leaves only $1.9M of cash
–	On conservative demand the lease loses $1.4M, 4.6 times its upside
Delivery, not insourcing, is the mandate; a second source protects it at lower cost
–	On-time delivery sits just under 97%, hurt by one flood closure
–	Four layers, from a second shop to reserved capacity, cover an outage
Buy with a second source in 2027 and switch to the lease only if a trigger fires
–	A 2028 lease is a near tie; orders, price or delivery would tip it
–	Renew the supplier contract before the quote lapses in March 2027

The margin above break-even is thin, and every assumption cuts toward it
▪	Planning demand of 300,000 is only 4.5% above break-even; the conservative 230,000 reaches 80% of it
▪	The supplier's $75 delivered price holds for three years, though it is quoted only to March 2027
▪	Lease scrap falls from 6% to 4% after 2027; if it stays at 6%, the three-year saving drops to $0.06M
▪	The lease runs all of 2027; a five-month deployment after a site survey means fewer units to spread its costs over
1  Break-even = costs to recover ÷ saving per good unit; 2027 scrap premium = 80,000 × ($52.13 − $51.04). Planning demand clears break-even by only about 13,000 units
Sources: Meridian Motion briefing pack; team analysis
